Honestly, I’m still trying to process the emotional weight of this show. I don't think I've ever felt this heavily, deeply attached to an anime before. Violet Evergarden isn't just something you watch for entertainment; it’s something you actively survive emotionally. It completely shatters your defenses, leaves you crying your eyes out, and then somehow patches you back together. The story follows Violet, a former child soldier who basically functions like a machine, as she becomes an "Auto Memoir Doll"—someone who writes letters for people who can't find the right words to express their feelings. Watching her journey from a blank slate trying to understand what"I love you" means, to someone who feels the deep, aching pain of human emotion, is just beautiful. The animation by Kyoto Animation is out of this world, and the orchestral soundtrack hits you right in the chest at the exact perfect moments.
But what really tore me apart was the underlying message about time. Every episode is a brutal, beautiful reminder of just how fragile our lives are. It makes you realize that tomorrow is never a guarantee. If there is one thing this show forces you to understand, it’s that today is the day you need to be with your loved ones. Don't wait. Tell them how you feel right now, because you never know if you'll get a tomorrow.
It’s an absolute masterpiece. If you're ready to let yourself be completely vulnerable and probably cry a river, please watch this. It will stay with you forever.

The show with the cumbersome title called "The Duke’s Son Claims He Won’t Love Me Yet Showers Me with Adoration" is neither good or bad. It is as average, as it can get and that is meant in a rather nice sort of way, really. When it comes to shoujo romance titles, I don't have high expectations anymore, since I've seen so many in all my years as anime watcher. So it doesn't take a lot to entertain me. And I felt entertained enough with this show, I would say. But it isn't in the slightest bit a memorable one. Neither the setting, nor the characters,nor the world in intself were anything new and it also failed to build a nice, refreshing twist on the trope of arranged marriages, where the characters learn to love each other over time. So, what's left to be loved about the show? Nothing much, to be honest.

We get a rather finished story in 12 episodes, but given the fact that nothing of great impact or any interesting slice of life ever happens, the show felt slow and aimless. There are attempts of building some sort of aristocratic rivalry and intrigue aside from the lovestory, but the characters lack real motivation and stakes. Instead, every conflict of that matter just vanishes into meaningless nothingness in the end.

While the female lead is an adorable, accepting and quietly outgoing person, the male lead leaves a bad taste in some aspects. He is cold and hurtful in the beginning, but eventually warms up at his wife's side. Nonetheless he is a spy for the crown (big word for the lack of worldbuilding here), always seeking information about opposing parties and uses every tool at hand for that - even if that means to use women and drop them after. The show doesn't go in a specific direction with it, but the implications are there. It's his job, sure, but in consideration of his past and "trauma", this leaves a real bad aftertaste. 

The world doesn't feel alive at all. Whenever there is a possibility for detail about the world, the conversations blend into music or into another scene. When our protagonists eventually are on a date, we get a power point slideshow of still images and bland music. On one of the most "romantic" scenes, we don't even get a real background anymore. Just blue with some colorful circles. Like there was no effort put in it at all or the budget ran out midway.

It's sad to see, really. It wasn't a horrible show, but it hadn't any good traits either. So I can't give anything above or below 5 here.
If you don't care about details and just want to kill some time, sure, go for it. But don't expect any quality or fresh twist on the trope. As long as you don't have high - or any - expectations, you're good to go. Otherwise I would recommend something else entirely.

data.review:
“No one in their right mind would do something as petty as stealing underwear!” ― Yuzuru Itsushiki, Cherry no Manma. Cherry no Manma is a shoujo romance anime based on a manga. This work can be described as a classic shoujo romance, but its plot has a unique twist: the story revolves around a misunderstanding involving a missing pair of girls' panties. However, the series contains no ecchi or so-called fan service, making it safe to watch with children. Cherry no Manma and Ano Ko ni 1000% were released as ten-minute bonuses at the end of the first and second LD/VHS of Umi no Yami, Tsuki no Kage, respectively. Bothprojects were produced by the same studio, and the teams that worked on them were almost identical. From a technical standpoint, Cherry no Manma is of higher quality.
The drawings are beautiful and detailed, and the animation is smooth.
The entire ten-minute OVA is filled with pleasant instrumental music that will appeal to any fans of late 80s romance anime.
The seiyuu's acting is nice.

The main strength of this anime is that very shoujo style from the turn of the 80s and 90s: both in technical terms, in terms of plot, and in terms of characters and tropes. If you absolutely love that style, go ahead and watch it; you’ll enjoy it.
However, there is nothing truly surprising or stunning about this work.

And most importantly, remember: this is an OVA. Moreover, it’s a ten-minute OVA. Don’t overthink and expect a coherent, clear explanation of what’s happening on screen; that would be the wrong approach to the genre. There is no clear and fixed opening, no definitive closure. Just riding on the feel train without stations of departure and arrival. The feel train and no boundaries. A small sip of feelings that helps you breathe.

Everything should be evaluated within the context of its genre and format. For a ten-minute shoujo romance OVA, this work is fine.

A powerful mage is sent back in time to undo a screwup. This show is a solid line of tropes played straight-up, and with decent execution it's enjoyable if you're a fan of them. There's a clear power fantasy aspect with semi-explicit power rankings, the MC concealing his power level, people underestimating him, etc. though that's only part of the focus. There's a magic academy and nobles that are pompous to the point of absurdity as well. Then there's the love interest who's literally named "romantica" and... yeah, it's about as tropey as you can get. The thing that makes this fun is that it's notabsurdly rushed like many other low-quality anime plotlines are, and the core group of the MC, the love interest, and the femboy sidekick have decent chemistry and are entertaining to watch. Their antics weren't hilarious but they did elicit a chuckle from me every now and then, which puts it leagues ahead of most anime. The show also has just enough of a meta story about the end of the world to not be totally unambitious.

It's a pretty simple show. If you like these sorts of tropes then this will give you a fill of them.

AND THE ENDING FELT UNEARNED. The magic path to victory was SUbaru remembering himself and the amnesia arc. Which was entirely pointless. To sum up the "Tetsunabe no Jan!" anime, which turned out to be another pleasant surprise of this year's summer season, it’s a cooking-and-rivalry series that feels like a hardcore version of Food Wars, even though the original manga dates back to 1995 (meaning there is a 31-year gap between the source material and this anime adaptation). Akiyama is a fascinating protagonist or rather, an anti-hero. He is arrogant, speaks his mind bluntly, and enjoys humiliating his opponents, driven by the philosophy that cooking is a form of combat. This stands in stark contrast to his rival, Kiriko, whose cooking is motivated by love and similarsentiments. I also appreciate that the series doesn't try to sugarcoat things; it remains a faithful adaptation of the original manga, which was uncompromising in its approach.

I give it an 8/10. It’s a great alternative to Food Wars that focuses more on rivalry than on discovering new flavors or techniques. It would be great if they announced another season, as there is plenty of source material for a continuation,though I might just pick up the manga itself, which is fully complete and even has a sequel series.

Is that a vampire in the Wild West? Hahahaha! Honestly, that was one of the first things that crossed my mind while watching this Blood Lad OVA. We have an extra adventure here that, while not significantly altering the main story's trajectory, serves as a sort of continuation of the anime's events, offering a few more moments with our characters and exploring the relationship between Staz and Fuyumi a bit further. The story follows Staz and Fuyumi as they wander the Demon World looking for a way to resolve the girl's situation; following previous events, she is dealing with the consequences of her supernatural condition and hascome to rely on Staz's blood. During this journey, they run into hunters pursuing the protagonist, sparking the conflicts that drive the special. It’s a relatively simple premise that uses the adventure as a backdrop to place the characters in new situations, without any grand narrative ambitions.

And honestly, I think that simplicity defines the experience perfectly. The OVA doesn't try to present an overly complex plot, build a massive mystery, or completely shift the series' direction. Its main goal seems to be simply delivering more of what made Blood Lad fun: comedy, absurd situations, supernatural elements, and, above all, the interaction between the protagonists.

Narratively speaking, there’s nothing particularly extraordinary here. The threat posed by the hunters drives the adventure, but the events lack the weight or depth to make the story truly memorable. It’s the kind of supplementary episode you watch casually, enjoying yourself while it plays, only to realize afterward that nothing particularly significant actually happened. It’s not bad, but it doesn't offer much for anyone hoping for something more ambitious.

On the other hand, the relationship between Staz and Fuyumi remains one of the most enjoyable aspects to watch. Staz has always been an interesting protagonist to me, primarily due to his blend of a carefree personality, unpredictable behavior, and obsession with human culture, especially anime, manga, and video games. He breaks away from the traditional image of the dark, intimidating vampire, functioning instead as a comic figure who, despite his powers, manages to be genuinely entertaining.

Seeing a bit more of him in this special was quite enjoyable, as was following his interactions with Fuyumi. Their relationship has a charm of its own, alternating between funny moments and cuter situations that keep the viewer engaged, even when the narrative doesn't offer anything groundbreaking. It is precisely this dynamic that sustains much of the episode and gives it value for existing fans of the series.

The comedy also deserves a mention. Blood Lad has always taken a laid-back approach to its supernatural universe, mixing demons, vampires, and other creatures with situations that often border on the absurd. The OVA maintains this identity, prioritizing immediate entertainment over complex narrative building. And, given the premise, this works reasonably well.

Even so, I feel something was missing to truly elevate this special. The concept is fun, the characters remain charismatic, and there are moments that make the experience worthwhile, yet everything feels a bit superficial. I would have liked to see a more memorable adventure, featuring more interesting conflicts or further development of the relationship between Staz and Fuyumi. Instead, we get a pleasant story, but one that hardly stands out when compared to the rest of the series.

In conclusion, this Blood Lad OVA is a fun addition for those who miss the characters, though it is far from essential. Its greatest strengths lie in the comedy and the interaction between Staz and Fuyumi, while its simple narrative prevents it from being anything more than fleeting entertainment. I recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the anime and wants to spend a little more time in that universe, but don't expect a story that will change your perception of the original work.

In the end, it’s fun, has its cute moments, and still raises the question: what the hell is a vampire doing in the Wild West? Hahahaha!

Rating: 6/10.

É um vampiro no faroeste? KKKKKKKKKKK

Sinceramente, essa é uma das primeiras coisas que me vieram à cabeça ao assistir a esse OVA de Blood Lad. Temos aqui uma aventura extra que, apesar de não alterar significativamente o rumo da história principal, serve como uma espécie de continuação dos acontecimentos do anime, trazendo mais alguns momentos com nossos personagens e explorando um pouco mais a relação entre Staz e Fuyumi.

A história acompanha Staz e Fuyumi enquanto os dois vagam pelo mundo demoníaco em busca de uma maneira de resolver a situação da garota, que, após os acontecimentos anteriores, enfrenta as consequências de sua condição sobrenatural e acaba dependendo do sangue de Staz. Durante essa jornada, eles se deparam com caçadores que estão atrás do protagonista, dando início aos conflitos que movimentam o especial. É uma premissa relativamente simples, que utiliza a aventura como pano de fundo para colocar os personagens em novas situações, sem grandes pretensões narrativas.

E, honestamente, acho que essa simplicidade define muito bem a experiência. O OVA não tenta apresentar uma trama extremamente elaborada, desenvolver um grande mistério ou mudar completamente a direção da obra. Sua principal intenção parece ser proporcionar mais um pouco daquilo que fez Blood Lad ser divertido: comédia, situações absurdas, elementos sobrenaturais e, principalmente, a interação entre seus protagonistas.

Narrativamente falando, não temos nada particularmente extraordinário. A ameaça dos caçadores serve como motor para a aventura, mas os acontecimentos não possuem tanto peso ou profundidade a ponto de tornar essa história especialmente memorável. É aquele tipo de episódio complementar que você acompanha tranquilamente, se diverte durante a exibição e, depois de terminar, percebe que não aconteceu nada tão marcante assim. Não chega a ser ruim, mas também não oferece muito para quem esperava algo mais ambicioso.

Por outro lado, o relacionamento entre Staz e Fuyumi continua sendo um dos pontos mais agradáveis de acompanhar. Staz sempre foi um protagonista interessante para mim, principalmente por essa mistura de personalidade despreocupada, comportamento imprevisível e obsessão pela cultura humana, especialmente por animes, mangás e videogames. Ele foge um pouco daquela imagem tradicional do vampiro sombrio e intimidador, funcionando muito mais como uma figura cômica que, apesar de seus poderes, consegue ser genuinamente divertida.

Ver um pouco mais dele neste especial foi bastante agradável, assim como acompanhar suas interações com Fuyumi. A relação dos dois possui um charme próprio, alternando momentos engraçados com situações mais fofas, que ajudam a manter o interesse mesmo quando a narrativa não apresenta grandes novidades. É justamente essa dinâmica que sustenta boa parte do episódio e faz com que ele tenha algum valor para quem já gosta da obra.

A comédia também merece destaque. Blood Lad sempre teve uma abordagem bastante descontraída de seu universo sobrenatural, misturando demônios, vampiros e outras criaturas com situações que frequentemente beiram o absurdo. O OVA mantém essa identidade, apostando mais no entretenimento imediato do que em uma construção narrativa complexa. E, considerando a proposta, isso funciona razoavelmente bem.

Ainda assim, sinto que faltou alguma coisa para elevar esse especial. A ideia é divertida, os personagens continuam carismáticos e existem momentos que justificam a experiência, mas tudo parece um pouco superficial. Gostaria de ter visto uma aventura mais marcante, com conflitos mais interessantes ou um desenvolvimento maior da relação entre Staz e Fuyumi. Em vez disso, ficamos com uma história agradável, mas que dificilmente se destaca quando comparada ao restante da obra.

Concluindo, este OVA de Blood Lad é um complemento divertido para quem sente falta dos personagens, mas está longe de ser indispensável. Sua maior qualidade está na comédia e na interação entre Staz e Fuyumi, enquanto sua narrativa simples impede que ele alcance algo além de um entretenimento passageiro. Recomendo para quem gostou do anime e quer passar mais um tempinho nesse universo, mas não esperem uma história capaz de mudar sua percepção da obra.

No fim, é divertido, tem seus momentos fofos e ainda rende a pergunta: o que diabos um vampiro está fazendo no faroeste? KKKKKKKKKKK!

Nota: 6/10.

data.review: Personal note - Watched almost every episode high af and my brain kept constantly thinking how everything shown here that wasn't explained can be modelled from our world today. The ideas of lonliness and disconnect in a world thats forever connected and the unexplained dread that there's something higher order controlling the way humans interact with each other was so ingrained in me as i kept watching episode by episode. I do not know what I went into it expecting, but i did come out with a lot many more questions. Definitely recommended for a weekend where you want spice and want to rack yourbrains out trying to figure out what is going on. The omnious vibe, dreadfully appropriate music and the ghostly visuals will keep you on the edge for every episode.

Fun, certainly, but not essential to the plot. Often regarded merely as an extra episode of the first season, this Oregairu OVA features another case involving the Service Club. This time, the protagonists receive a request from their teacher to help organize an event promoting marriage, aiming to introduce and discuss the topic among young people. The premise is actually interesting—especially since it allows for an exploration of issues regarding relationships and the characters' feelings, but, honestly, I didn't find anything particularly extraordinary here. Starting with the episode's concept, I find the choice of theme interesting. After all, this is a series that deals precisely with thecomplexities of human relationships, social expectations, and how young people view love. Using marriage as a starting point could have led to compelling discussions, particularly given the love triangle developing between Hachiman, Yukino, and Yui. However, despite this potential, the special doesn't delve as deeply into these issues as it could have. The subject serves more as a pretext to place the characters in specific situations than as a foundation for a truly impactful discussion.

That said, this doesn't mean the episode is bad. On the contrary, seeing the Service Club handle another request is quite enjoyable, especially for those who already appreciate the dynamic between the main characters. The humor still works, and the interactions between them provide some entertaining moments. Hachiman, with his cynical view of social relations, remains a primary source of entertainment, while Yukino and Yui contribute to the conflicts and situations that drive the episode forward.

Another point worth mentioning is the character design. Since this is a 2013 production, it retains the visual style of the first season, something that tends to divide fan opinion, especially when compared to the style adopted in later seasons. Personally, I don't consider the old character design bad. It has its own charm and fits the visual identity of that phase of the adaptation, even though I do prefer the more recent look. In any case, it doesn't detract from my experience with the special.

What really counts against the OVA is its limited narrative relevance. Although the episode gives more room to the dynamic between the three protagonists and adds a few moments to their relationships, there aren't enough significant events to justify watching it if you are interested solely in the main plot. It is the kind of supplementary content that works best for those already invested in the characters who simply want to spend more time following their interactions.

However, revisiting Oregairu after so much time also offered me a slightly different experience. Beyond the nostalgia, it was interesting to realize how my own worldview has shifted since I first encountered the series. When I was younger, I found it much easier to agree with Hachiman’s pessimism, viewing his cynical take on human relationships as quite logical. Today, though, I realize just how naive that line of thinking can be, especially when it turns negative experiences into a justification for distrusting others and avoiding any form of vulnerability.

And I believe that is precisely one of the most interesting aspects of Oregairu: the series isn't just about presenting a pessimistic protagonist who supposedly sees truths that everyone else ignores. The female characters, especially Yukino and Yui, help challenge that worldview, each in her own way, highlighting that relationships are far more complex than simply avoiding disappointment or trying to find rational explanations for feelings. It is in this contrast of perspectives that the story finds much of its strength, even when the episode falls short of exploring these themes with the desired depth. Ultimately, this OVA is a pleasant, fun, and nostalgic supplement, though it doesn't quite reach the level of significance found in the series' best moments. It offers a few more interactions between familiar characters, explores a theme that could have sparked interesting discussions, and reinforces aspects of the story's romantic dynamic. However, it lacks that special something to truly set it apart from a standard episode or make the story leave a lasting impression.

I’d say it’s a special worth checking out if you enjoy Oregairu and miss following Hachiman, Yukino, and Yui, just don't expect major revelations, significant plot shifts, or exceptional depth added to the love triangle. It is a pleasant bonus episode that fulfills its purpose of entertaining, even though it is far from essential.

Rating: 6/10.

Muitas vezes considerado apenas um episódio extra da primeira temporada, este OVA de Oregairu apresenta mais um caso envolvendo o Clube de Serviços Voluntários. Dessa vez, os protagonistas recebem um pedido de sua professora para ajudarem na organização de um evento voltado à promoção do casamento, com o objetivo de apresentar e discutir esse tema entre os jovens. A premissa até é interessante, principalmente porque permite explorar algumas questões relacionadas aos relacionamentos e aos sentimentos dos personagens, mas, sinceramente, não achei nada particularmente extraordinário aqui.

Começando pela proposta do episódio, considero interessante a escolha do tema. Afinal, estamos falando de uma obra que trabalha justamente com as dificuldades dos relacionamentos humanos, as expectativas sociais e a maneira como os jovens enxergam o amor. Utilizar o casamento como ponto de partida poderia render discussões interessantes, especialmente considerando o triângulo amoroso que se desenvolve entre Hachiman, Yukino e Yui. Entretanto, apesar desse potencial, o especial não aprofunda tanto essas questões quanto poderia. O assunto serve mais como um pretexto para colocar os personagens em determinadas situações do que como base para uma discussão realmente marcante.

Ainda assim, isso não significa que o episódio seja ruim. Pelo contrário, rever o Clube de Serviços Voluntários lidando com mais um pedido é algo bastante agradável, principalmente para quem já gosta da dinâmica entre os protagonistas. O humor continua funcionando, e as interações entre eles conseguem proporcionar alguns momentos divertidos. Hachiman, com sua visão cínica das relações sociais, continua sendo uma das principais fontes de entretenimento, enquanto Yukino e Yui contribuem para os conflitos e as situações que movimentam o episódio.

Outro ponto que merece ser mencionado é o design dos personagens. Por se tratar de uma produção de 2013, ainda temos o visual da primeira temporada, algo que costuma dividir opiniões entre os fãs, especialmente quando comparado ao estilo adotado nas temporadas posteriores. Particularmente, não considero o design antigo ruim. Ele possui seu próprio charme e combina com a identidade visual daquela fase da adaptação, embora eu realmente prefira o visual mais recente. De qualquer maneira, não é algo que prejudique minha experiência com o especial.

O que realmente pesa contra o OVA é sua pouca relevância narrativa. Embora o episódio dê mais espaço para a dinâmica entre os três protagonistas e acrescente algumas situações ao relacionamento deles, não temos acontecimentos suficientemente importantes para justificar sua visualização caso você esteja interessado exclusivamente na trama principal. É aquele tipo de conteúdo complementar que funciona melhor para quem já está envolvido com os personagens e deseja passar mais algum tempo acompanhando suas interações.

Entretanto, revisitar Oregairu depois de tanto tempo também me proporcionou uma experiência um pouco diferente. Além da nostalgia, foi interessante perceber como minha própria visão de mundo mudou desde a época em que tive contato com a obra. Quando era mais novo, conseguia concordar muito mais facilmente com o pessimismo de Hachiman, enxergando sua maneira cínica de interpretar as relações humanas como algo bastante coerente. Hoje, porém, percebo o quanto esse raciocínio também pode ser ingênuo, especialmente quando transforma experiências negativas em justificativas para desconfiar das pessoas e evitar qualquer tipo de vulnerabilidade.

E acredito que esse seja justamente um dos aspectos mais interessantes de Oregairu: a obra não se resume a apresentar um protagonista pessimista que supostamente enxerga verdades que os outros ignoram. As personagens femininas, especialmente Yukino e Yui, ajudam a confrontar essa visão de mundo, cada uma à sua maneira, evidenciando que os relacionamentos são muito mais complexos do que simplesmente evitar decepções ou tentar encontrar respostas racionais para os sentimentos. É nesse contraste de perspectivas que a história encontra boa parte de sua força, mesmo quando o episódio não consegue explorar tudo isso com a profundidade desejada.

No fim, este OVA é um complemento simpático, divertido e nostálgico, mas que não chega a alcançar o mesmo nível de relevância dos melhores momentos da série. Ele oferece mais algumas interações entre personagens que já conhecemos, trabalha com um tema que poderia render discussões interessantes e reforça aspectos da dinâmica romântica que acompanha a obra. Contudo, falta algo que realmente o diferencie de um episódio comum ou que faça sua história permanecer na memória depois de assistida.

Concluo que é um especial que vale a pena conferir se você gosta de Oregairu e sente falta de acompanhar Hachiman, Yukino e Yui, mas não espere grandes revelações, mudanças significativas na trama ou um aprofundamento excepcional do triângulo amoroso. É um episódio extra agradável, que cumpre sua função de entreter, embora esteja longe de ser indispensável.

Nota: 6/10.

Rin: Daughters of Mnemosyne is a gorey, horny trip--a popcorn flick of an anime that I found myself thoroughly enjoying. The animation is not good. 2000s nostalgia only gets you so far when the art direction is weak. Character design is meh, lighting is meh, environment design is meh--the art is very typical for the time period. Some of the fashion choices were also really hit or miss. OST is okay. The best part of this show is Rin’s suit, and I’m not kidding. The vignette plot structure is at least interesting; the loosely-connected short stories spread over nearly a 100 years fit very wellwith an immortal protagonist. The characters themselves are fine---I love the agency Rin has, and her more mature personality. She moves through the world with a tired grace that I find extremely compelling. Despite her years, she is not inhuman; Rin retains humility, emotion, and passion, even if she rarely shows those sides of herself. Rin retains the will to keep moving forward, regardless of how she’s beaten down. In essence, she is the ideal female whumpee, if you know what that means. Mimi is okay. I can’t say I care very much for her. Kouki is similarly fine. 

Beyond Rin, this is a fairly standard mystery-thriller, with a fuck ton of rape, tits, and gore. There’s a good balance between whump and plot, but the plot is not very exhilarating. I just couldn’t really get into the story beyond mere curiosity on what the world had to offer. IDK, just didn’t do it for me. This was a very easy watch, which is usually a bad thing in my case. 

If nothing else, this show has an excellent dub. Colleen Clikenbeard as Rin, Todd Haberkorn as Apos, Jamie Marchi as Mimi, Clarien Harp as Laura, Luci Christian as Mishio, and Robert McCollum as Kouki all did an excellent job of bringing this anime to life. Funimation Dub Studio, I miss you dearly. 

The ending is not good. I didn’t love the bio-essentialist theming towards the end, and the final episode as a whole felt really rushed. Things felt so quick that I barely understood the mystery’s answer towards the end, and nor did I really care to know. 

I am not this show’s target audience, but I didn’t hate it. It’s not a show that’ll change your life, but it’s a fun, pulpy action flick that draws you in. Mostly, I love independent female characters. It’s a relatively unique show that may be worth your time.

There’s something about this anime that makes me want to stay in its world a little longer. I really love the atmosphere of this anime. The way it portrays magic, nature, and folklore makes everything feel so peaceful yet mysterious. Sometimes, I don't even need anything major to happen. Just watching the scenery, listening to the music, and seeing the little interactions between the characters is enough to keep me interested. I also like how the story explores Chise and Elias as individuals who are still learning about themselves and others. Their relationship is far from perfect, but seeing them slowly learn about emotions and human connectionsis one of the things that makes this anime interesting to me.

It's not an anime for everyone, though. The pacing can be slow, and some parts might feel a little confusing. But personally, I don't mind that much because I enjoy the world it builds and the little details scattered throughout the story.

Overall, this anime gives me a kind of comfort that's difficult to explain. It makes me want to walk through a quiet forest, discover something magical, and forget about the world for a while.

It's definitely one of those anime that makes me wish I could experience its world for myself.
